You could have heard a pin drop.

During a break, one of the French engineers came back into the room saying, "Have you heard the latest dumb stunt Bush has done? He has sent an aircraft carrier to Indonesia to help the tsunami victims. What does he intend to do, bomb them?" A Boeing engineer stood up and replied quietly: "Our carriers have three hospitals on board that can treat several hundred people; they are nuclear powered and can supply emergency electrical power to shore facilities; they have three cafeterias with the capacity to feed 3,000 people three meals a day, they can produce several thousand gallons of fresh water from sea water each day, and they carry half a dozen helicopters for use in transporting victims and injured to and from their flight deck. We have eleven such ships. How many does France have?"
You could have heard a pin drop.
A U.S. Navy admiral was attending a naval conference that included admirals from the U.S., English, Canadian, Australian, and French navies at a cocktail reception. He found himself standing with a large group of officers that included personnel from most of those countries. Everyone was chatting away in English as they sipped their drinks when a French admiral suddenly complained that, whereas Europeans learn many languages, Americans learn only English. He then asked, "Why is it that we always have to speak English in these conferences rather than speaking French?" Without hesitating, the American admiral replied, "Maybe it's because the Brits, Canadians, Aussies, and Americans arranged it so you wouldn't have to speak German."
You could have heard a pin drop.

Robert Whiting, an elderly gentleman of 83, arrived in Paris by plane. At French customs, he took a few minutes to locate his passport in his carry on. "You have been to France before, monsieur?" the customs officer asked sarcastically. Mr. Whiting admitted that he had been to France previously. "Then you should know enough to have your passport ready." The American said, "The last time I was here, I didn't have to show it." "Impossible. Americans always have to show their passports on arrival in France!" The American senior gave the Frenchman a long hard look. Then he quietly explained, ''Well, when I came ashore at Omaha Beach on D-Day in 1944 to help liberate this country, I couldn't find a single Frenchmen to show a passport to."
You could have heard a pin drop.

items.tx:
During the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, Ukrainian military personnel also evacuated 167 civilians from the right bank of Kherson Oblast

During the ceasefire regime introduced in designated areas of Kherson Oblast for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, the Defense Forces of Ukraine utilized the opportunities created by the security situation to evacuate residents from the right bank of Kherson Oblast.

This refers to settlements in the territory controlled by Ukraine along the Dnipro River, which faced daily shelling by the army of russia. Those who previously had no opportunity to leave the dangerous areas were able to depart.

Specifically, the civil-military cooperation units of the "South" Group of Forces, in cooperation with local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer locations in Kherson Oblast. Among them were 22 children and 21 mobility-impaired individuals who required special attention and assistance.

It is worth noting that the evacuation took place under extremely difficult and dangerous conditions. The routes passed through mined roads that suffered destruction, areas with burned military equipment and civilian cars. All of this significantly complicated movement and required special caution and coordinated actions of all involved units.

Despite these risks, the main priority remains saving the lives of the civilian population and providing assistance to those who cannot independently leave the dangerous territories.

Every saved person is the result of joint work and coordinated interaction of all those involved in the humanitarian mission.

Units of the "South" Group of Forces clearly and strictly adhere to the ceasefire regime in the area of the humanitarian mission.
